title: When should a short-lived certificate renew?
answer: renew at a share of the certificate’s life, not a fixed time before expiry

checks.question: A CA issues 20-day certificates, and Certbot keeps renew_before_expiry at 30 days. How many certificates does it get in a year, and how many would the 4.1 default get?
checks.answer: With the 30-day setting, 264 renewed and 465 runs refused, the first at hour 84, exactly as for 160-hour certificates: any certificate shorter than 30 days is due from issue, so every run asks until the limit refuses. The default renews two thirds of the way through, since 20 days is not under ten: at day 13.3, 27 times a year.

checks.question: For 45-day certificates, someone sets renew_before_expiry to 10 days. When does Certbot 4.1 renew, and how long is left to retry?
checks.answer: At day 35, the first twice-daily run within 10 days of expiry, leaving 20 runs to retry. The setting replaces the default rather than adding to it: without it Certbot would renew at day 30 with 30 runs to spare.

checks.question: A client renews at a random time inside Let’s Encrypt’s ARI window. Is that order exempt from the 5-in-7-days limit?
checks.answer: Not by its timing alone. Boulder exempts an order only when it names the certificate it replaces and arrives inside that certificate’s window. Certbot 5.8’s orders name no predecessor, so they are counted even when they follow the window.

steps.caption: Each bar is one certificate, from issue to expiry, drawn to one time scale and lined up at expiry. The highlighted line is the 30-day test: renew once expiry is less than 30 days away. The tick at the start of each 30-day bracket marks where that test starts to pass: 30 days before the right-hand end of each bar. On a 90-day certificate that is day 60, with a third of its life left. A 160-hour certificate is shorter than the margin: its due point falls 560 hours, 23.3 days, before it was issued. It is due from the moment it exists, so the first twice-daily run, at hour 12, replaces it, and the replacement is due from issue too.

steps.title: Certbot 4.1 renews half way through a 160-hour certificate
steps.line: Half of 160 hours is hour 80, renewed by the run at hour 84; the 30-day rule renews at hour 12.
steps.caption: Certbot 4.1 changed the rule: renew at a share of the certificate’s life, not a fixed time before expiry. With renew_before_expiry unset, it renews two thirds of the way through, or half way under ten days, unless the CA sends an ARI answer, a renewal window of its own (RFC 9773). A fraction scales with the lifetime; a fixed number of days does not. Thirty days is longer than a 160-hour certificate’s whole life, so under the old rule every run tries to renew; the new one waits until hour 80.

steps.title: 160 hours under the 30-day rule: 13 renewals in two weeks
steps.line: Every run renews until hour 84; then most are refused.
steps.caption: Each tick after the first is a renewal, counted at the right, over two weeks from a first certificate on 1 March 2028. Under the 30-day rule a certificate is due from issue, since 30 days is longer than its life, so even a fresh replacement is already due under the same rule. Every run renews until, at hour 84, Let’s Encrypt starts refusing most runs (the short marks under the strip, counted as refused). Later ticks are 24 to 36 hours apart.
steps.picture: A two weeks axis from 1 March 2028 with one strip of ticks. 30 days before expiry: a first certificate on 1 March, then 13 renewals in two weeks, at hour 12, hour 24, hour 36 and so on; 14 runs refused, the first at hour 84.

steps.title: Certbot 4.1+ default: 3 renewals instead
steps.line: In 365 days: 264 under the 30-day rule, 104 under the default rule.

steps.title: Renewing at every run, Let’s Encrypt refuses at hour 84
steps.line: 5 per 7 days, one back every 33.6 h; 465 refused in 365 days.
steps.caption: Let’s Encrypt allows 5 certificates for the same names in 7 days and gives one back every 33.6 hours. After 6 renewals the run at hour 84 is refused; in 365 days 465 runs are refused and 264 renew.

steps.title: Certbot’s renewals still count against the limit
steps.line: Certbot’s order names no predecessor, so the limit check runs.
steps.caption: Boulder skips the 5-in-7-days check only for an order that names the certificate it replaces and arrives inside that certificate’s ARI window. Certbot 5.8’s order carries identifiers and a profile and names no predecessor, so its renewals are checked. The renewal window and this exemption are different: following the window does not itself name the replaced certificate. A refused order costs nothing; an issued certificate takes a token.

steps.title: Let’s Encrypt’s ARI window: hour 78.9 to hour 82.1
steps.line: The 30-day setting renews at hour 12, before the window opens.
steps.caption: Certbot 4.1 and later ask Let’s Encrypt when to renew; its ARI answer is a window 1% of the life either side of half way. The 30-day setting still renews on its own, at hour 12, before the window opens, so the answer changes nothing until the setting is removed.
